glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Conflict with the Pharisees grows as Jesus shows mercy on the Sabbath, is revealed as Isaiah’s gentle Servant, overcomes Satan by the Spirit of God, warns against blasphemy against the Spirit, promises the sign of Jonah, and names those who do the Father’s will as His family.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Matthew 12 continues the third movement, The King Meets Rejection and Recognition. The rest Jesus offered in 11:28–30 now meets disputes over the Sabbath in Galilee.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Matthew 12:1–8 — Lord of the Sabbath

  • Matthew 12:9–14 — Healing a Withered Hand on the Sabbath

  • Matthew 12:15–21 — The Chosen Servant of Isaiah’s Prophecy

  • Matthew 12:22–32 — The Beelzebub Accusation and Blasphemy against the Spirit

  • Matthew 12:33–37 — Good and Bad Trees and the Words of the Heart

  • Matthew 12:38–42 — The Sign of Jonah

  • Matthew 12:43–45 — The Return of the Unclean Spirit

  • Matthew 12:46–50 — Jesus’ True Family

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you.” (Matthew 12:28)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Two Sabbath disputes open the chapter. When the Pharisees accuse His hungry disciples, Jesus answers from Scripture, declares that One greater than the temple is here, quotes Hosea again, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (12:7), and claims to be Lord of the Sabbath. He heals a man’s withered hand in the synagogue, and the Pharisees plot to destroy Him. Matthew then sets Isaiah’s portrait beside Jesus: the Spirit-anointed Servant who will not break a bruised reed or quench smoking flax, and in whose name the Gentiles will trust.

When Jesus frees a man who was blind, mute, and demon-possessed, the crowds wonder whether He is the Son of David. The Pharisees say He works by Beelzebub. Jesus answers that He casts out demons by the Spirit of God, so the kingdom has come upon them, and the strong man is being bound. Calling the Spirit’s plain testimony to Christ satanic is the path to the sin that will not be forgiven: willful, conscious, final rejection of the Spirit’s revelation of Jesus. The rest of the chapter searches the heart through words, the demand for signs, the danger of an empty house, and the joy of belonging to Jesus’ family.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Matthew 12:1–8 — Lord of the Sabbath

When the Pharisees object that His disciples pluck grain on the Sabbath, Jesus answers from David, the priests, and Hosea. He declares that One greater than the temple is here and that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.

Matthew 12:9–14 — Healing a Withered Hand on the Sabbath

In the synagogue Jesus heals a man’s withered hand, teaching that it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath. The Pharisees go out and plot to destroy Him.

Matthew 12:15–21 — The Chosen Servant of Isaiah’s Prophecy

Jesus withdraws, heals many, and tells them not to make Him known. Matthew sees Isaiah 42:1–4 fulfilled in the gentle Servant who brings justice to victory and hope to the Gentiles.

Matthew 12:22–32 — The Beelzebub Accusation and Blasphemy against the Spirit

Jesus heals a blind and mute demon-possessed man, and the Pharisees claim He works by Beelzebub. Jesus shows that He casts out demons by the Spirit of God, binds the strong man, and warns that blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.

Matthew 12:33–37 — Good and Bad Trees and the Words of the Heart

A tree is known by its fruit, and the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart. People will give account for their idle words on the day of judgment.

Matthew 12:38–42 — The Sign of Jonah

When the scribes and Pharisees demand a sign, Jesus promises only the sign of Jonah: the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. Nineveh and the queen of the South will condemn a generation that ignores One greater than Jonah and Solomon.

Matthew 12:43–45 — The Return of the Unclean Spirit

An unclean spirit that leaves a man and finds the house empty returns with seven worse spirits. Jesus applies this warning to His wicked generation.

Matthew 12:46–50 — Jesus’ True Family

When His mother and brothers seek Him, Jesus points to His disciples. Whoever does the will of His Father in heaven is His brother, sister, and mother.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Matthew 12 shows that the kingdom has arrived in power. Jesus’ deliverances are real rescues, the strong man is bound, and Satan’s captives are freed by the Spirit of God. The same chapter shows the King’s tenderness. He does not discard the bruised or the faltering, and His gentleness gives weak people reason to come to Him.

The chapter also brings comfort to anxious consciences. The unpardonable sin is not a stray thought or a fearful question. The Pharisees’ accusation shows its direction, a deliberate calling of the Spirit’s work evil, though the chapter does not say each of them had reached final rejection. Grief over sin and a desire to turn to Jesus are reasons for reassurance, and anyone who comes to Him may receive forgiveness (1 John 1:9).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Mercy and the Sabbath. Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath and does good on it (12:7–8, 12).

The gentle Servant. Isaiah’s Servant restores the bruised and brings justice to victory (12:18–21).

Kingdom power. Jesus binds the strong man by the Spirit of God (12:28–29).

Words and the heart. Speech reveals the heart and will be judged (12:34–37).

True family. Doing the Father’s will marks Jesus’ family (12:49–50).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Lord of the Sabbath (12:8). Jesus has authority over the day God gave, and He interprets it by God’s mercy.

Bruised reed and smoking flax (12:20). Pictures from Isaiah of what is weak and nearly finished. The Servant does not crush the damaged or put out a faint flame.

Beelzebub (12:24). A name used for Satan, the ruler of the demons. The Pharisees use it to accuse Jesus.

Blasphemy against the Spirit (12:31). The willful, conscious, and final rejection of the Spirit’s revelation of Christ. It refuses the only testimony through which a person comes to the Savior.

Three days and three nights (12:40). Jesus’ time in the grave, compared to Jonah’s time in the fish. Jesus was buried on Thursday afternoon, and the annual and weekly Sabbaths passed before He rose by Sunday dawn. Others count it in the Jewish inclusive way from a Friday. Either way, Jesus truly died, was buried, and rose.

focus: Matthew 12 shows opposition to Jesus hardening as the Pharisees challenge Him over the Sabbath, plot how they might destroy Him, and attribute His casting out of demons to Beelzebub. Matthew presents Jesus as the Lord of the Sabbath and the gentle Servant of Isaiah’s prophecy, and Jesus answers His opponents with warnings about blasphemy against the Spirit, the words that come from the heart, the sign of the prophet Jonah, and the danger of an empty house, before naming those who do His Father’s will as His family.

sections.title: Lord of the Sabbath
sections.summary: When the Pharisees accuse Jesus’ disciples of doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath by plucking heads of grain, Jesus answers from what David did and from the priests’ service in the temple. He declares that One greater than the temple is here, that God desires mercy and not sacrifice, and that “the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Matthew 12:8).

sections.title: Healing a Withered Hand on the Sabbath
sections.summary: In the synagogue Jesus is asked whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, and He answers that if they would lift a sheep out of a pit, it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath. He restores the man’s withered hand, and the Pharisees go out and plot against Him, “how they might destroy Him” (Matthew 12:14).

sections.title: The Chosen Servant of Isaiah’s Prophecy
sections.summary: Knowing their plot, Jesus withdraws, heals all who follow Him, and warns them not to make Him known. Matthew says this fulfills Isaiah’s prophecy of God’s chosen Servant, upon whom He puts His Spirit, who will not quarrel or cry out, will not break a bruised reed or quench smoking flax, and in whose name Gentiles will trust.

sections.title: The Beelzebub Accusation and Blasphemy against the Spirit
sections.summary: When Jesus heals a demon-possessed man who is blind and mute, the multitudes ask whether this could be the Son of David, but the Pharisees say He casts out demons by Beelzebub. Jesus answers that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand, that if He casts out demons by the Spirit of God the kingdom of God has come upon them, that no one can plunder a strong man’s goods unless he first binds the strong man, and that blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.

sections.title: Good and Bad Trees and the Words of the Heart
sections.summary: Jesus declares that a tree is known by its fruit and that “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34). He warns that people will give account for every idle word in the day of judgment, for by their words they will be justified or condemned.

sections.title: The Sign of Jonah
sections.summary: When some of the scribes and Pharisees ask for a sign, Jesus answers that no sign will be given to an evil and adulterous generation except the sign of the prophet Jonah: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth. The men of Nineveh and the queen of the South will rise up in the judgment and condemn this generation, for One greater than Jonah and Solomon is here.

sections.title: The Return of the Unclean Spirit
sections.summary: Jesus describes an unclean spirit that leaves a man, finds the house empty, swept, and put in order, and returns with seven other spirits more wicked than itself, so that the last state of that man is worse than the first. He concludes, “So shall it also be with this wicked generation” (Matthew 12:45).

sections.title: Jesus’ True Family
sections.summary: When Jesus is told that His mother and brothers are outside seeking to speak with Him, He stretches out His hand toward His disciples and says, “Here are My mother and My brothers!” (Matthew 12:49). He declares that “whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother” (Matthew 12:50).

1.brief: On a Sabbath Jesus goes through the grainfields, and His hungry disciples begin to pick heads of grain and eat. The scene sets up a conflict over what faithful Sabbath observance requires.
1.explain:
“At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath.”

Jesus had just offered rest to the weary (11:28–30). Now a conflict arises over the “Sabbath,” the day of rest God gave Israel. The Sabbath was the seventh day of the week, set apart for rest and worship (Exodus 20:8–11).

“And His disciples were hungry, and began to pluck heads of grain and to eat.”

The disciples are “hungry.” As they walk along the paths through the fields, they pick some heads of grain, rub them in their hands, and eat. The law allowed travelers to pick grain by hand from a neighbor’s field (Deuteronomy 23:25).
1.notes: Luke 6:1 adds that they rubbed the grain in their hands.

2.brief: The Pharisees object, “Look, Your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath!” They treat picking grain as forbidden work and hold Jesus responsible for His disciples.
2.explain:
“And when the Pharisees saw it,”

The Pharisees are watching closely.

“they said to Him, ‘Look, Your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath!”

The Pharisees do not object to picking grain. They object to doing it on the Sabbath. Their traditions counted plucking grain as reaping and rubbing it as threshing. Both were forbidden work on the Sabbath. Jesus is responsible for His disciples, so they bring the charge to Him.
2.notes: The law forbade work on the Sabbath (Exodus 20:10) but did not define every kind of work. Jewish tradition later listed thirty-nine categories of forbidden work, including reaping and threshing.

3.brief: Jesus asks whether they have not read what David did when he and his companions were hungry. He answers their charge from Scripture.
3.explain:
“But He said to them, ‘Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him:”

Jesus answers from Scripture. The Pharisees were experts in the Scriptures. Jesus asks whether they have understood what they read. He points them to an event in the life of “David,” Israel’s greatest king.

4.brief: David entered God’s house and ate the showbread, which only the priests were permitted to eat. Scripture itself records that human need took precedence over a ceremonial rule in David’s case.
4.explain:
“how he entered the house of God and ate the showbread”

David was fleeing from Saul. He came to the tabernacle at Nob and asked the priest for food. The only bread available was the “showbread,” the twelve loaves placed before the LORD each Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–9).

“which was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests?”

The law reserved the showbread for the priests. Yet the priest gave it to David and his men because they were hungry. Scripture does not condemn him. Human need took priority over a ceremonial rule.

If David, the anointed king, could do this, how much more can the disciples of the Son of David?
4.notes: The house of God here refers to the tabernacle, which was at Nob at that time.

5.brief: Jesus adds that the priests in the temple work on the Sabbath and yet are blameless. The law itself requires temple service that would otherwise count as Sabbath work.
5.explain:
“Or have you not read in the law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath, and are blameless?”

Jesus gives a second example, this time from the law itself. The priests work in the temple on the Sabbath. They offer sacrifices and replace the showbread (Numbers 28:9–10). Technically they break the Sabbath rest, yet they are “blameless.” The service of God in the temple takes priority.
5.notes: Rabbis taught that temple service overrode the Sabbath.

6.brief: Jesus declares that “in this place there is One greater than the temple.” If temple service justifies Sabbath work, the presence of One greater than the temple carries even greater authority.
6.explain:
“Yet I say to you that in this place there is One greater than the temple.”

Jesus makes a bold claim. If temple service justified the priests’ work, then service to Jesus justifies His disciples. He is greater than “the temple.”

The temple was the place of God’s presence. Jesus is claiming something greater. In Him, God Himself is present (1:23).
6.notes: The Greek word translated “One greater” is neuter, something greater. It may refer to Jesus Himself or to the kingdom present in Him.

7.brief: Had they understood “I desire mercy and not sacrifice,” they would not have condemned the guiltless. Quoting Hosea 6:6 again, Jesus shows that God values mercy above ritual strictness and that His disciples are innocent.
7.explain:
“But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,”

Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 again, as He did in 9:13. God values “mercy” above ritual. The Pharisees knew the law, but they did not know God’s heart.

“you would not have condemned the guiltless.”

If they had understood God’s desire for mercy, they would not have condemned the disciples. Jesus calls His disciples “guiltless.” They have done nothing wrong.
7.notes: Hosea 6:6 continues: “And the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.”

8.brief: Jesus concludes, “For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.” He has the authority to declare the Sabbath’s true meaning because He is its Lord.
8.explain:
“For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.”

Jesus is “Lord” of the Sabbath. God gave the Sabbath. Jesus has authority over it. He decides what honors it.

Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath here. He restores its purpose. Mark 2:27 records His words: the Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath.
8.notes: Hebrews 4:9–10 speaks of a Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God, entered through faith in Christ.

9.brief: Leaving there, Jesus goes into their synagogue. The Sabbath debate continues in a place of worship.
9.explain:
“Now when He had departed from there, He went into their synagogue.”

Jesus goes into the local “synagogue,” the place where Jews gathered for prayer and the reading of Scripture on the Sabbath.
9.notes: Luke 6:6 says this took place on another Sabbath.

10.brief: A man with a withered hand is there, and they ask Jesus whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, hoping to accuse Him. They use a suffering man as bait for a legal trap.
10.explain:
“And behold, there was a man who had a withered hand.”

In the synagogue is a man with a “withered hand.” His hand was shriveled or paralyzed. Luke 6:6 says it was his right hand, the hand he would need for work.

“And they asked Him, saying, ‘Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?’—that they might accuse Him.”

The Pharisees ask a question to set a trap. Their goal is “that they might accuse Him.” Their tradition allowed medical help on the Sabbath only if a life was in danger. This man’s condition was not life-threatening. If Jesus healed him, they could accuse Him of breaking the Sabbath.
10.notes: Mark 3:2 and Luke 6:7 say they watched Him closely to see whether He would heal on the Sabbath.

11.brief: Jesus asks which of them would not grab hold of a sheep that fell into a pit on the Sabbath and lift it out. Their own practice shows mercy to animals on the Sabbath.
11.explain:
“Then He said to them, ‘What man is there among you who has one sheep, and if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not lay hold of it and lift it out?”

Jesus answers with a question from everyday life. If a man’s only sheep fell into a pit on the Sabbath, would he leave it there? No. Even the Pharisees would rescue it.
11.notes: Some Jewish groups forbade lifting an animal out of a pit on the Sabbath. Most allowed it or allowed food to be given to the animal until the next day.

12.brief: Since a man is worth much more than a sheep, “it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” The Sabbath is a day for doing good to people in need.
12.explain:
“Of how much more value then is a man than a sheep?”

A person is worth far more than an animal. If they would help a sheep, they should certainly help a man.

“Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.”

Jesus draws the conclusion. The Sabbath is a day for doing good. Mercy toward human need honors God’s day.
12.notes: Mark 3:4 records Jesus asking whether it is lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil, to save life or to kill.

13.brief: Jesus tells the man, “Stretch out your hand,” and as he does, it is restored as whole as the other. Jesus’ word heals the man in front of His accusers, demonstrating what He has just taught.
13.explain:
“Then He said to the man, ‘Stretch out your hand.”

Jesus speaks to the man and gives a simple command. He does not touch him. He only speaks.

“And he stretched it out, and it was restored as whole as the other.”

The man obeys. As he stretches out his hand, it is healed. It becomes as healthy as his other hand. Jesus’ word brings restoration.
13.notes: Jesus does no work that the Pharisees could call a breach of their rules. He only speaks, and the man stretches out his hand.

14.brief: The Pharisees go out and plot how they might destroy Him. Confronted with mercy and power, they respond with murderous hostility.
14.explain:
“Then the Pharisees went out and plotted against Him, how they might destroy Him.”

The Pharisees respond with hatred. They leave the synagogue and plot “how they might destroy Him.” They are angry that Jesus healed on the Sabbath, yet they plan murder on the same day.

This is a turning point. The opposition has moved from criticism to a plan to kill Jesus.
14.notes: Mark 3:6 says the Pharisees plotted with the Herodians, supporters of Herod’s family.

15.brief: Knowing the Pharisees’ plot to destroy Him, Jesus withdraws, and great crowds follow Him, and He heals them all. He does not retaliate against His enemies but continues His work of mercy.
15.explain:
“But when Jesus knew it, He withdrew from there.”

Jesus knows about the plot, and He leaves the area. His time to die has not yet come.

“And great multitudes followed Him, and He healed them all.”

Large crowds follow Him, and He heals “them all.” The Pharisees plot to destroy. Jesus continues to restore.
15.notes: Matthew often records Jesus withdrawing from danger (2:14; 4:12; 14:13).

16.brief: Jesus warns those He heals not to make Him known, and Matthew explains the warning by what follows in Isaiah’s portrait of the quiet Servant.
16.explain:
“Yet He warned them not to make Him known,”

Jesus tells those He healed not to publicize Him. He does not seek fame or stir up a political movement.

17.brief: Jesus’ withdrawal, healing, and warning fulfill what Isaiah the prophet spoke. Matthew shows that these match Scripture’s portrait of God’s Servant.
17.explain:
“that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaiah the prophet, saying:”

Matthew explains that Jesus’ quiet way of working fulfills Isaiah’s prophecy about God’s Servant.
17.notes: The quotation in 12:18–21 comes from Isaiah 42:1–4. It is the longest Old Testament quotation in Matthew.

18.brief: Isaiah writes, “Behold! My Servant whom I have chosen, My Beloved in whom My soul is well pleased!” God puts His Spirit on Him, and He will proclaim justice to the Gentiles. The Father’s words at Jesus’ baptism echo here, identifying Jesus as the Spirit-anointed Servant whose mission reaches the nations.
18.explain:
“Behold! My Servant whom I have chosen,”

God speaks of “My Servant.” God has chosen Him for a special task. Matthew identifies Jesus as this Servant.

“My Beloved in whom My soul is well pleased!”

God calls the Servant “My Beloved” and says He is “well pleased” with Him. These words echo the Father’s voice at Jesus’ baptism (3:17).

“I will put My Spirit upon Him,”

God’s “Spirit” rests on the Servant. At Jesus’ baptism the Spirit descended on Him like a dove (3:16).

“And He will declare justice to the Gentiles.”

The Servant will bring “justice” to the nations. His mission reaches beyond Israel. Justice here means God’s right order, His saving rule.
18.notes: The Greek word translated “justice” can also be translated judgment.

19.brief: The Servant will not quarrel or cry out, and no one will hear His voice in the streets. Jesus does not seek His goals through self-promotion or angry confrontation.
19.explain:
“He will not quarrel nor cry out,”

The Servant is not aggressive or loud. He does not argue or shout to gain attention.

“Nor will anyone hear His voice in the streets.”

He does not seek publicity. This explains why Jesus withdrew and told people not to make Him known (12:15–16).
19.notes: Jesus does speak boldly when He confronts sin (23:13–36). The point here is that He does not stir up crowds or seek fame.

20.brief: “A bruised reed He will not break, And smoking flax He will not quench,” until He brings justice to victory. Jesus is gentle with the weak and faltering, restoring rather than discarding them, while His saving purpose moves on to certain triumph.
20.explain:
“A bruised reed He will not break,”

A “bruised reed” is a damaged stalk, bent and almost broken. Most people would snap it off and throw it away. The Servant does not.

“And smoking flax He will not quench,”

“Smoking flax” is a lamp wick that is almost out. It gives more smoke than light. Most people would put it out. The Servant does not.

These images picture people who are weak, wounded, and failing. Jesus does not discard them. He restores them. Believers who are damaged or whose faith has grown faint can come to Him. He draws them back to His Word, to prayer, to repentance, and to life in the Spirit. He renews what is almost gone.

“Till He sends forth justice to victory;”

His gentleness is not weakness. He will bring “justice to victory.” He will complete His mission and establish God’s rule. His gentleness serves His victorious purpose.
20.notes: The images are pictures, not a description of how every weak believer came to be weak. Isaiah 42:3 reads, “A bruised reed He will not break, And smoking flax He will not quench; He will bring forth justice for truth.”

21.brief: “And in His name Gentiles will trust.” The Servant’s mission offers hope to the nations.
21.explain:
“And in His name Gentiles will trust.”

The nations will put their hope in the Servant. Even as Israel’s leaders reject Jesus, Matthew points to the time when the Gentiles will trust in Him.
21.notes: Isaiah 42:4 in Hebrew reads that the coastlands will wait for His law. Matthew follows the Greek translation, which reads that the Gentiles will hope in His name.

22.brief: A demon-possessed man who is blind and mute is brought to Jesus, and He heals him so that he both speaks and sees. Jesus frees the man from demonic bondage and restores his sight and speech.
22.explain:
“Then one was brought to Him who was demon-possessed, blind and mute;”

A man is brought to Jesus who is under demonic oppression and cannot see or speak.

“and He healed him, so that the blind and mute man both spoke and saw.”

Jesus heals him completely. The man can now speak and see. Jesus frees the captive.

23.brief: The crowds are amazed and ask, “Could this be the Son of David?” They begin to wonder whether Jesus is the promised Messiah.
23.explain:
“And all the multitudes were amazed and said, ‘Could this be the Son of David?”

The crowds are astonished. They ask whether Jesus might be “the Son of David,” the Messiah. Their question expects that the answer may be yes. They are beginning to wonder.
23.notes: The Greek form of the question suggests hesitation, as if they hardly dare believe it.

24.brief: The Pharisees say that He casts out demons only by Beelzebub, the ruler of the demons. Unable to deny the deliverance, they attribute God’s work to Satan.
24.explain:
“Now when the Pharisees heard it they said,”

The Pharisees hear the crowd’s question. They must respond, because the people are beginning to believe.

“This fellow does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, the ruler of the demons.”

They cannot deny the miracle. So they attribute it to “Beelzebub, the ruler of the demons,” Satan himself. They repeat the charge of 9:34. They call God’s work the work of the devil.

25.brief: Knowing their thoughts, Jesus says that every kingdom, city, or house divided against itself cannot stand. He exposes the absurdity of their charge.
25.explain:
“But Jesus knew their thoughts, and said to them:”

Jesus knows what they are thinking and answers them.

“Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand.”

Jesus states a principle everyone knows. A kingdom fighting itself will fall. A city or a family torn by internal conflict will not last.
25.notes: Mark 3:24–25 and Luke 11:17 record the same saying.

26.brief: If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself, and his kingdom could not stand. Satan would not destroy his own work.
26.explain:
“If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself.”

Jesus applies the principle. If Satan were casting out his own demons, he would be fighting against himself.

“How then will his kingdom stand?”

Satan would be destroying his own kingdom. The accusation makes no sense.
26.notes: Jesus speaks of Satan as having a kingdom, an organized realm of evil.

27.brief: If Jesus casts out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do their own sons cast them out? Their own people, who practice exorcism, will judge the inconsistency of their accusation.
27.explain:
“And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?”

Jesus turns the question back on them. Some of the Pharisees’ own followers practiced exorcism. If Jesus casts out demons by Satan, what about them?

“Therefore they shall be your judges.”

Their own disciples would condemn their reasoning. The Pharisees are applying a double standard.
27.notes: Acts 19:13–16 mentions Jewish exorcists who traveled from place to place.

28.brief: But if Jesus casts out demons by the Spirit of God, “surely the kingdom of God has come upon you.” His deliverances by the Spirit show that God’s reign is breaking in among them.
28.explain:
“But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God,”

Jesus states the true source of His power. He casts out demons “by the Spirit of God.” This fulfills the prophecy just quoted: God has put His Spirit on His Servant (12:18).

“surely the kingdom of God has come upon you.”

If Jesus casts out demons by God’s Spirit, then God’s kingdom “has come upon you.” God’s rule is present and active in Jesus. His victory over demons is the evidence.
28.notes: Luke 11:20 says by the finger of God. The phrase recalls Exodus 8:19, where Pharaoh’s magicians recognized the finger of God.

29.brief: No one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods without first binding the strong man. Jesus has overpowered Satan and is setting his captives free.
29.explain:
“Or how can one enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man?”

Jesus gives a picture. “The strong man” is Satan. His “goods” are the people he holds captive. No one can rob a strong man’s house without first tying him up.

“And then he will plunder his house.”

Jesus is stronger than Satan. He has bound him and is freeing those Satan held captive. Every person delivered from demonic power is evidence that Jesus has overpowered the enemy.
29.notes: Isaiah 49:24–25 asks whether the prey can be taken from the mighty and answers that the LORD will contend with him and save His people.

30.brief: Whoever is not with Jesus is against Him, and whoever does not gather with Him scatters. No one can remain neutral toward Jesus and His work.
30.explain:
“He who is not with Me is against Me,”

There is no neutral ground. A person either stands with Jesus or against Him. The Pharisees claim to serve God, but by opposing Jesus they oppose God.

“and he who does not gather with Me scatters abroad.”

Jesus is gathering God’s people. Those who do not gather with Him scatter. They work against His mission.
30.notes: In Mark 9:40 Jesus says, “he who is not against us is on our side.” That saying concerns someone casting out demons in Jesus’ name. This one concerns those who oppose Him.

31.brief: Because the Pharisees have called the deliverance Jesus does by the Spirit the work of Satan, He warns that every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. God’s forgiveness is vast, yet there is a rejection that places a person beyond it.
31.explain:
“Therefore I say to you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men,”

Jesus makes a wide promise. “Every sin” can be forgiven. Even blasphemy, speaking against God, can be forgiven.

“but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven men.”

There is one exception. In this scene the Pharisees saw the Spirit’s work in delivering a captive and deliberately called it the work of Satan. They willfully inverted what they saw.

Blasphemy against the Spirit is the willful, conscious, and final rejection of the Spirit’s revelation of Christ. The Spirit bears witness to Jesus (John 15:26), and there is no other Savior (Acts 4:12). The one who finally refuses the Spirit’s testimony refuses the only way of forgiveness.
31.notes: Mark 3:30 explains that Jesus said this because they said, “He has an unclean spirit.”

32.brief: A word spoken against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but speaking against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven in this age or the age to come. Blasphemy against the Spirit is the willful, conscious, and final rejection of the Spirit’s testimony to Christ, the very testimony that leads people to the Savior; a person grieved over sin and wanting to turn to Jesus has not committed it.
32.explain:
“Anyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him;”

Speaking against Jesus can be forgiven. People who misunderstood Him, mocked Him, or even opposed Him could later repent and believe. Paul had been a blasphemer and persecutor, yet he received mercy (1 Timothy 1:13).

“but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, either in this age or in the age to come.”

Speaking against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven. This is not a careless word or a moment of doubt. It is the settled rejection of the Spirit’s witness to Jesus.

A person who grieves over sin and wants to turn to Jesus has not committed this sin. That desire is itself the Spirit’s work. An intrusive thought, a fearful question, or a careless remark is not, by itself, this final rejection. God promises to forgive all who confess their sins (1 John 1:9).
32.notes: The phrase this age or the age to come is a Jewish expression meaning never.

33.brief: Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for a tree is known by its fruit. What people say and do reveals what they really are.
33.explain:
“Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or else make the tree bad and its fruit bad;”

Jesus uses a familiar picture. A tree and its fruit match. A good tree produces good fruit. A bad tree produces bad fruit.

“for a tree is known by its fruit.”

The fruit reveals the tree. The Pharisees’ words against the Spirit reveal what is in their hearts.
33.notes: Jesus used the same picture in the Sermon on the Mount to warn against false prophets (7:16–20).

34.brief: Jesus calls the Pharisees a “Brood of vipers!” and asks how evil people can speak good things, for “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” Their slander of the Spirit’s work exposes the evil in their hearts.
34.explain:
“Brood of vipers! How can you, being evil, speak good things?”

Jesus calls the Pharisees “Brood of vipers,” offspring of poisonous snakes. John the Baptist used the same words (3:7). Because their hearts are evil, they cannot speak good things.

“For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”

Words come from the heart. What fills the heart overflows in speech. The Pharisees’ words reveal the evil inside them.

35.brief: A good person brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart, and an evil person brings evil things out of evil treasure. Words flow from what is stored within.
35.explain:
“A good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good things,”

The heart is like a storehouse of “treasure.” A good person has stored up good things, and good things come out.

“and an evil man out of the evil treasure brings forth evil things.”

An evil person has stored up evil, and evil comes out. What is stored in the heart eventually shows itself.

36.brief: People will give account on the day of judgment for every idle word they speak. Even careless words matter to God because they reveal the heart.
36.explain:
“But I say to you that for every idle word men may speak,”

An “idle word” is a careless or useless word, spoken without thought.

“they will give account of it in the day of judgment.”

Even careless words matter to God. Every person will “give account” for them. Words matter because they reveal the heart that produces them.
36.notes: The Greek word translated “idle” means inactive or worthless.

37.brief: “For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” A person’s words will bear witness in God’s judgment to the true condition of his heart.
37.explain:
“For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”

Words will serve as evidence in the judgment. They show what is truly in the heart. A person is not saved by speaking good words. But words reveal whether the heart has been changed by God.
37.notes: James 3:2–12 warns of the power of the tongue.

38.brief: Some scribes and Pharisees say, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from You.” Despite all they have seen, they demand still more proof.
38.explain:
“Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered, saying,”

Some of the religious leaders respond to Jesus’ warning.

“Teacher, we want to see a sign from You.”

They ask for a “sign,” a miracle that would prove His authority. They have just seen Him heal a blind and mute man. Their request shows unbelief, not a desire to know the truth.
38.notes: In 16:1 the Pharisees and Sadducees ask for a sign from heaven.

39.brief: Jesus says that an evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and none will be given except the sign of the prophet Jonah. He refuses to perform on demand for those unfaithful to God.
39.explain:
“But He answered and said to them, ‘An evil and adulterous generation seeks after a sign,”

Jesus describes the people of His day as evil and unfaithful. In the Old Testament, adultery often pictures unfaithfulness to God (Hosea 2:2–5). They demand signs while refusing to believe the signs they have already seen.

“and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.”

Jesus refuses to perform a sign on demand. The only sign they will receive is “the sign of the prophet Jonah.”

40.brief: As Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. The decisive sign will be Jesus’ own burial and resurrection.
40.explain:
“For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish,”

Jesus explains the sign. Jonah spent three days and nights inside a great fish (Jonah 1:17). Then he came out alive.

“so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.”

Jesus will be in the grave for the same length of time, and then He will rise. His death and resurrection will be the great sign.

Counting these days most naturally places Jesus’ crucifixion on Thursday, before a special Passover Sabbath that fell on Friday, followed by the weekly Sabbath on Saturday. This gives three nights and three days in the tomb, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, before the women found the tomb empty at dawn on Sunday (28:1–6). Other faithful interpreters explain the phrase by the Jewish custom of counting any part of a day as a whole day.
40.notes:
The Greek word translated “great fish” can refer to any large sea creature. Jonah 1:17 says that the LORD prepared a great fish.

John 19:31 says that the Sabbath after the crucifixion was a high day.

41.brief: The men of Nineveh will rise in the judgment and condemn this generation, because they repented at Jonah’s preaching, and One greater than Jonah is here. Pagan Nineveh repented at a lesser messenger’s word, so this generation’s refusal is without excuse.
41.explain:
“The men of Nineveh will rise up in the judgment with this generation and condemn it,”

The people of “Nineveh,” the capital of Assyria, will testify against Jesus’ generation at the final judgment.

“because they repented at the preaching of Jonah;”

Nineveh was a pagan city. Yet when Jonah preached, they repented (Jonah 3:5–10).

“and indeed a greater than Jonah is here.”

Jonah was a reluctant prophet who preached only judgment. Jesus is far greater. If Nineveh repented at Jonah’s preaching, how much more should Israel repent at Jesus’ preaching.
41.notes: The Greek word translated “a greater” is neuter, as in 12:6.

42.brief: The queen of the South will also rise in the judgment and condemn this generation, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and One greater than Solomon is here. A foreign queen traveled far to hear wisdom, while these leaders reject the greater wisdom standing before them.
42.explain:
“The queen of the South will rise up in the judgment with this generation and condemn it,”

This queen is the queen of Sheba. She came from a distant land in the south, probably southern Arabia.

“for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon;”

She made the long journey to test and hear Israel’s wise king (1 Kings 10:1–10).

“and indeed a greater than Solomon is here.”

Jesus is greater than Solomon, Israel’s wisest king. She traveled far to hear Solomon. Jesus’ generation will not listen to the One standing among them.
42.notes: Jesus has now claimed to be greater than the temple (12:6), greater than Jonah the prophet (12:41), and greater than Solomon the king (12:42).

43.brief: When an unclean spirit leaves a man, it wanders through dry places seeking rest and finds none. Jesus begins a warning about deliverance that is not followed by a new life.
43.explain:
“When an unclean spirit goes out of a man,”

Jesus tells a short story about a demon that leaves a person.

“he goes through dry places, seeking rest, and finds none.”

The demon wanders through “dry places,” the desert, which was considered a home of evil spirits. It finds no rest.
43.notes: Isaiah 13:21 and Isaiah 34:14 picture desolate places as the haunt of wild creatures.

44.brief: The spirit decides to return to the house it left, and finds it empty, swept, and put in order. The house has been cleaned, but nothing has filled it.
44.explain:
“Then he says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.”

The demon decides to return to the person it left, whom it calls “my house.”

“And when he comes, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order.”

The house is “empty.” It has been cleaned and tidied, but no one lives in it. Something bad has been removed, but nothing good has taken its place.
44.notes: The point is the emptiness. The house is clean but unoccupied.

45.brief: The spirit brings seven others worse than itself, and the man’s last state is worse than the first; “So shall it also be with this wicked generation.” Jesus applies the warning to this generation, which has seen God’s deliverance but has not received Him, and the principle shows that only a life filled by the King is secure.
45.explain:
“Then he goes and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter and dwell there;”

The demon brings “seven other spirits” worse than itself. Seven is the number of completeness. The person is completely overtaken.

“and the last state of that man is worse than the first.”

The person ends up worse off than before. Outward improvement without a new inner life leaves a person open to worse bondage.

“So shall it also be with this wicked generation.”

Jesus applies the story to “this wicked generation.” Israel had been blessed by the ministry of John and Jesus. But if they reject Jesus, their condition will be worse than before.

The warning also applies to individuals. Reform is not enough. A heart must be filled with God’s presence through receiving Jesus.
45.notes: 2 Peter 2:20 makes a similar point about those who escape the pollutions of the world and are again entangled in them.

46.brief: While Jesus is still speaking to the crowds, His mother and brothers stand outside wanting to speak with Him. His natural family seeks His attention.
46.explain:
“While He was still talking to the multitudes,”

Jesus is still teaching the crowds.

“behold, His mother and brothers stood outside, seeking to speak with Him.”

Jesus’ “mother” Mary and His “brothers” arrive. They stand outside and want to speak with Him. Mark 3:21 says that His family had come to take Him home because they thought He was out of His mind.
46.notes: Jesus’ brothers are named in 13:55: James, Joses, Simon, and Judas. John 7:5 says that His brothers did not believe in Him at that time. James later became a leader in the church at Jerusalem (Acts 15:13).

47.brief: Someone tells Him that His mother and brothers are outside seeking to speak with Him. The message gives Jesus the occasion for His teaching about His true family.
47.explain:
“Then one said to Him, ‘Look, Your mother and Your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak with You.”

Someone tells Jesus that His family is outside.
47.notes: Some manuscripts do not include this verse.

48.brief: Jesus asks, “Who is My mother and who are My brothers?” His question points beyond natural family ties.
48.explain:
“But He answered and said to the one who told Him,”

Jesus answers the person who brought the message.

“Who is My mother and who are My brothers?”

Jesus asks a question that redefines family. He does not reject His earthly family. He uses this moment to teach about a deeper family.
48.notes: On the cross Jesus entrusted His mother to the care of John (John 19:26–27).

49.brief: Stretching out His hand toward His disciples, He says, “Here are My mother and My brothers!” Jesus names His followers as His family.
49.explain:
“And He stretched out His hand toward His disciples and said,”

Jesus points to “His disciples,” those who follow Him.

“Here are My mother and My brothers!”

His disciples are His family. They are bound to Him by a relationship deeper than blood.
49.notes: Hebrews 2:11 says that Jesus is not ashamed to call them brethren.

50.brief: Whoever does the will of His Father in heaven is His brother and sister and mother. Doing the Father’s will marks those who belong to Jesus’ family, a bond deeper than any natural tie.
50.explain:
“For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother.”

Jesus defines His true family. It is made up of those who do “the will of My Father.” Anyone, man or woman, can belong. Doing the Father’s will marks a person as part of Jesus’ family.

Doing God’s will does not earn a place in the family. It shows that a person belongs. It begins with believing in the One God sent (John 6:29).

These family members are the brethren of Jesus whom He will mention in 25:40.
50.notes: Jesus adds sister, though only His brothers are mentioned as standing outside. Women are fully included in His family.
